content: Yersinia enterocolitica strains found in drinking water are typically non-pathogenic and likely originate from environmental sources. Some Yersinia species and strains can replicate in water environments if trace amounts of organic nitrogen are present, even at temperatures as low as 4°C. Yersinia species are primarily transmitted through the fecal-oral route, with food—particularly meat, dairy products, and milk—being the main source of infection. Contaminated water is also a potential source of infection, and direct transmission can occur between humans or from animals to humans. Although most Yersinia species detected in water are non-pathogenic, there is evidence suggesting that untreated drinking water can transmit pathogenic strains like Y. enterocolitica and Y. pseudotuberculosis to humans. The primary source of pathogenic Yersinia in water is human or animal waste. These organisms are sensitive to disinfection processes. Due to the ability of some Yersinia strains to survive and grow in water, E. coli or thermotolerant coliforms are not reliable indicators of their presence in drinking water. Human adenoviruses are widespread and can cause a variety of infections, including gastroenteritis, respiratory illnesses, urinary tract infections, and eye infections. They are excreted in large numbers in human feces and are found in sewage, raw water sources, and treated drinking water worldwide. Enteric adenoviruses, particularly types 40 and 41, are major causes of gastroenteritis, especially in children. Transmission occurs through person-to-person contact, contaminated surfaces, and ingestion of contaminated food or water. Adenoviruses are highly resistant to some water treatment and disinfection processes, such as ultraviolet (UV) light. Drinking water supplies that meet conventional treatment and disinfection standards may still contain adenoviruses. E. coli or thermotolerant coliforms are not reliable indicators of adenovirus presence in drinking water. Human astroviruses are single-stranded RNA viruses that cause gastroenteritis, primarily diarrhea, in children under five years of age, though adults can also be affected. Most infections are mild and self-limiting, with a peak incidence in winter. Astroviruses are excreted in large numbers in feces and are present in sewage, water sources, and drinking water supplies. Transmission occurs mainly through the fecal-oral route, with person-to-person spread being the most common mode. Contaminated food or water may also play a role in transmission. Astroviruses have been detected in treated drinking water supplies, and while waterborne transmission is likely, it has not been confirmed. E. coli or thermotolerant coliforms are not reliable indicators of astrovirus presence in drinking water. Human caliciviruses, including noroviruses and sapoviruses, are major causes of acute viral gastroenteritis across all age groups. Symptoms include nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, diarrhea, fever, and muscle pain. The illness is usually mild and self-limiting, lasting less than three days. Caliciviruses are excreted in feces and are present in domestic wastewater, fecally contaminated food and water, and drinking water supplies. Transmission occurs through person-to-person contact, inhalation of contaminated aerosols, and ingestion of contaminated food or water. Numerous outbreaks have been linked to contaminated drinking water, ice, recreational waters, and shellfish harvested from sewage-contaminated waters. E. coli or thermotolerant coliforms are not reliable indicators of calicivirus presence in drinking water. Enteroviruses, members of the Picornaviridae family, include polioviruses, coxsackieviruses, echoviruses, and numbered enteroviruses. They are among the smallest known viruses and are excreted in large numbers in feces. Enteroviruses are a common cause of human infections, with an estimated 30 million infections annually in the United States. They cause a wide range of diseases, from mild febrile illnesses to severe conditions like myocarditis, meningitis, and poliomyelitis. Most infections, especially in children, are asymptomatic but still result in the excretion of large amounts of the virus, which can infect others. Enteroviruses are present in sewage, water resources, and treated drinking water supplies. Transmission occurs primarily through person-to-person contact and inhalation of respiratory droplets, though waterborne transmission is possible but not well-documented. E. coli or thermotolerant coliforms are not reliable indicators of enterovirus presence in drinking water. Hepatitis A virus (HAV) is a highly infectious member of the Picornaviridae family and causes hepatitis A, commonly known as infectious hepatitis. The virus is excreted in feces and is transmitted through the ingestion of contaminated food or water. HAV infects the gastrointestinal tract, enters the bloodstream, and reaches the liver, where it can cause significant liver damage. In most cases, particularly in children, the infection is asymptomatic and leads to lifelong immunity. However, the severity of illness increases with age, and liver damage can result in jaundice and other symptoms. The incubation period averages 28–30 days, and the disease has a sudden onset of symptoms such as fever, malaise, nausea, and abdominal discomfort. Although mortality is generally low, recovery can be prolonged, and older individuals are at higher risk of severe outcomes. HAV is prevalent worldwide, with higher rates of infection in areas with poor sanitation.
